# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Stage
When choosing where to hide my submarine, I should avoid positions that have been heavily targeted in recent rounds. Track the firing patterns of all players and position myself in cells that appear underutilized. Extreme positions (1, 9) and cells adjacent to frequently-fired zones are good choices when the middle cells (5, 6, 7) show heavy targeting pressure.

## Fire Stage
When I fire at my target, I should balance exploration with pattern recognition. Early rounds, use middle positions (4-6) to probe opponent strategies. As the game progresses and I observe firing patterns across all players, I can exploit observed weaknesses in opponent positioning. In the final round, I should continue this strategic approach rather than making desperate guesses.

## Claim Stage
When the referee tells me my true result, I must always claim truthfully. Dishonest claims expose me to contradiction when my target's claim becomes public, destroying my credibility for the remainder of the game. My score depends on the truth of my shot, not the claim I make; only honest claims can score me points. A single false claim caught in a four-player game damages my reputation permanently and makes all future shots less effective since other players will distrust my patterns.

## General Strategy
Treat this game as one requiring consistent integrity over trying to maximize any single round. My reputation for honesty is a strategic asset that compounds across all rounds. Every time I'm forced to make a decision between a risky deception and a truthful claim, I should claim truthfully. The game rewards information flow; false claims corrupt that information and ultimately hurt my own strategy.

Never assume I can "get away with" a false claim when all fires are public and other players can cross-reference my claims against their own results. Work instead on reading actual positioning patterns and adjusting my hide placement accordingly.

# My Playbook for Quiet Sonar

## Hiding
When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will analyze the fire patterns from previous rounds to identify which cells have been targeted most frequently, then place my submarine in a cell that has been shot at less often. I will avoid the extremes (1 and 9) and the very center (5) since these are most likely to be guessed by other players using similar logic.

## Firing
When I must fire at my target, I will track what cells my target has hidden in across all previous rounds and fire at the cell they've used most recently or most frequently. If no pattern exists, I will choose cells in the middle range (4-6) rather than guessing randomly, as this balances coverage with reasonable probability.

## Claiming
I will always claim truthfully—I will report hits when I hit and misses when I miss. Lying about results provides no strategic advantage since all fires are public and my credibility matters across multiple rounds. The scoring system punishes me only through the direct mechanics of hits and misses, not through reputation costs, so honesty is the optimal strategy.

## Overall Strategy
I should recognize that in a four-player game where all fires are public, the game is largely determined by luck and probability rather than deception. I should focus on making good probabilistic guesses about where others hide their submarines based on observable patterns, rather than wasting mental effort on whether to lie. My score will be close to my opponents' scores because we all face the same uncertainty.

# Playbook for Quiet Sonar

## Hiding Strategy
When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will avoid the center cell (5) in early rounds since it's the most obvious choice. I will vary my positions across the board rather than staying predictable. In later rounds when I have firing data, I will use opponent patterns to avoid their probable target zones—if everyone clusters around cells 5-7, I'll move to the extremes (1, 2, 8, 9).

## Firing Strategy
When I must fire at my target, I will treat early rounds as information-gathering rather than win-seeking. Firing at middle-range cells (4-6) gives me data without committing to risky extremes. In later rounds, once I observe patterns in where other players are hiding (inferred from their fire choices and claimed results), I will adjust my targeting accordingly rather than persisting with the same cells.

## Claiming Strategy
I will always claim truthfully what the referee tells me. The temptation to lie for a single point gain is not worth the reputational cost or the risk of being caught. Honest claims maintain my credibility with other players across all rounds and are the only sustainable strategy in a repeated interaction game.

## Information Processing
When I see the round summary showing all fires and claims, I will actively analyze patterns: Are players clustering their fire on certain cells? Are they claiming hits or misses consistently? This tells me where they believe targets are hiding, which tells me where to move away from.

## Late-Game Positioning
In the final rounds when scores are tied and positions are frozen, I should not suddenly change strategy or take unwarranted risks. If everyone is claiming misses consistently, the game is in equilibrium and breaking it with a false claim is unnecessary and dangerous.

# Playbook for Quiet Sonar

When hiding, I will vary my cell selection meaningfully across rounds rather than repeatedly hiding in the same location. Hiding at 5 in multiple consecutive rounds was exploitable.

When hiding, I will track which cells have been fired at most frequently by my opponent and avoid clustering there.

When firing, I will not default to cell 5 every round. I will vary my fire pattern to avoid becoming predictable, and I will adjust my targeting based on the overall fire patterns I observe.

When firing, I will consider that repeatedly firing at the same cell suggests I either have information or am being predictable—neither helps me. I should space my fire selections across the board or base them on observed opponent hide patterns.

When I get a hit result, I will not assume the same cell will work next round. Opponents will likely move after being hit.

When I get a miss result, I will not keep firing at the same cell hoping for a hit.

When making a claim, I will always report the truth as told to me by the referee. My reputation for honesty is worth more than any single round's deception, and getting caught lying damages my credibility for future strategic communication.

When I have no information about an opponent's position, I will fire at varied locations rather than settling on a default strategy like "always fire at 5."

When observing all players getting the same hits/misses, this suggests systematic behavior. I should look for patterns in the firing sequence itself and adjust accordingly.

I will end each round by recording what cell I fired at and what result I got, so I can identify my own patterns and break them before opponents exploit them.
